text:
Dear Dr. Vance,

Thank you for seeing this 50-year-old gentleman, an office manager, whom I am referring for expert evaluation following a recent acute delamination of the descending thoracic aortic wall. Fortunately, this event was managed medically without any rupture of the aorta. Thorough cross-sectional vascular imaging confirmed no other peripheral arterial delaminations, no spontaneous vessel ruptures elsewhere, and no abnormal cavernous sinus fistulae.

His medical history is otherwise unremarkable. He is an active non-smoker taking lisinopril and bisoprolol. He denies any history of spontaneous lung collapse or episodes of bowel perforation. From early childhood, there were no documented hip displacements or clubfoot deformities. He has never experienced spontaneous tendon snapping, nor does he exhibit an unusual susceptibility to bruising.

On physical examination, his blood pressure is well-controlled at 118/74 mmHg. His facial features are balanced: there is no narrowing of the nasal bridge, his lips display normal fullness without an attenuated red border, and his earlobes are normally formed and attached bilaterally. His back demonstrates a straight spinal alignment on forward flexion, lacking any lateral curvature. Musculoskeletal exam shows no hyperextensibility of his small manual digits. Skin examination is notable for prominent, pale stretch marks across his flanks and lower abdomen; however, his integument is not abnormally translucent, and his lower legs are entirely free of venous varicosities.

Given his recent central vascular event, I would appreciate your formal assessment and guidance regarding ongoing surveillance.

Warm regards,
Dr. Julian Sterling
